registers.role: linkage of employees to their firms; occupation and industry used to define workplaces and the white-collar/private-sector restrictions

linkages: The three registers are merged to obtain annual information on Danish employees and their matched firms from 1996 to 2001
Employees are grouped into 'workplaces': all employees with the same two-digit ISCO occupation code in the same firm
Employee-level savings are observed in both employer sponsored (401(k)-like) and private (IRA-like) accounts, which allows the employer/individual comparison
Earnings and pension contributions are third-party reports from employers and pension funds to the tax authority

sample.universe: Danish wage earners aged 20-60 in private-sector firms and white-collar occupations, 1996-2001
sample.unit_of_observation: workplace-year (two-digit occupation-firm cell by year); the summary statistics and the private-account comparisons also use worker-year observations
selection_rules: exclude individuals under age 20 or over age 60
focus on the 20 percent of workers outside collective bargaining agreements by excluding workers in the public sector or in blue-collar occupations
exclude observations of workers with self-employment income
exclude occupation-firm cells with fewer than five employees
for the Figure 2 comparison, additionally exclude employees with earnings below the top tax threshold
for the Figure 4 optimality analysis, additionally restrict to workplaces whose entire workforce was above the top income tax threshold and whose 1998 default capital contribution rate was positive
sample.n_observations: 84,764 workplace-year observations; 2,020,705 worker year observations (60,643 workplace-year observations in the specifications with income controls)
sample.n_individuals: 26,775 unique workplaces (the number of unique individuals is not reported)

construction_notes: Contribution rates to employer sponsored accounts are measured as contribution levels divided by taxable labor income
The employer contribution rate (the 'default') is the median contribution rate within a two-digit occupation-firm cell in a given year; modes are used as a robustness check in online Appendix A
A 'workplace' is a two-digit occupation-firm cell; occupations are differentiated at the two-digit ISCO level
The main outcome is the change in the employer contribution rate from year t-1 to year t
Regression coefficients are multiplied by 100 to convert them into percentage point units
Standard errors are clustered at the workplace level (clustering at the firm level does not change significance patterns)
Income controls are a fifth-order polynomial of mean workplace-level labor income, separately for workers above and below the top tax threshold, interacted with year indicators

In Table 1 all monetary values are nominal Danish Kroner (exchange rate approximately DKr 6.5 per US$1), labor income is total pre-tax wage earnings plus employer pension contributions, pension contribution levels are winsorized at the 99th percentile, and the pre-reform values are from 1998
In Figure 4 the extensive-margin series are computed among units with positive capital contributions in 1998

definition.value: In 1999 the reform reduced the average deduction for contributions to capital pensions from 59 cents per DKr to 45 cents per DKr for individuals in the top income tax bracket, leaving the deduction for lower-bracket workers and for annuity contributions unchanged

timing.value: The reform took effect in 1999; outcomes observed annually 1996-2001 with 1998 as the last pre-reform year

outcome.label: Fraction of individuals who opted out of private (IRA-like) capital pension contributions, among those with positive private capital contributions in 1998

register_source.value: income tax register (pension contributions reported directly by pension funds to the tax authority)

definition.value: One minus the plotted time series of the fraction of individuals with positive private capital contributions among those who had positive private contributions in 1998 (the series marked by circles in Figure 4)

timing.value: Annual series 1996-2001, normalised on those with positive contributions in 1998

units.value: percent of the relevant 1998 population with positive capital contributions that had opted out by 2001

magnitude.interpretation: opt out of them, with an overall opt-out rate of approximately 50 percent by 2001.

estimand.target_population: Individuals above the top income tax threshold with positive private capital contributions in 1998
estimand.time_horizon: share having opted out by 2001, with 1998 (the last pre-reform year) as the reference year

population.description: Individuals with income above the top income tax threshold, in white-collar occupations in the private sector, who had positive private capital pension contributions in 1998
population.selection: individuals above the top income tax threshold who were directly affected by the reform; white-collar occupations in the private sector; self-employed excluded; restricted to those with positive private capital contributions in 1998

identification.source_of_variation: The 1999 reform, which cut the capital-pension deduction for top-bracket workers; Figure 4 plots the extensive-margin time series of positive capital contributions, 1996-2001, for units that had positive contributions in 1998

key_assumptions.assumption: The year-to-year movement in the plotted series around 1999 reflects the reform rather than other contemporaneous shocks; the pre-reform years 1996-1998 serve as the implicit benchmark
key_assumptions.supported_by: Flat or uniform pre-reform series in the same figures

key_assumptions.assumption: The median contribution rate within an occupation-firm cell identifies the employer-set default, so the plotted changes are employer rather than employee choices
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix A (modes instead of medians, bunching of employee rates at the workplace aggregate, zero-annuity-default workplaces, varying minimum cell size)

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on private-sector white-collar workplaces with at least five employees, used as a proxy for jobs outside collective bargaining agreements
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix D argues that inadvertently including collectively bargained workers only attenuates the estimates

implies_edges.from: private-sector white-collar workplace with at least five employees (sample inclusion)
implies_edges.to: employer capital pension contributions

key_assumptions.assumption: The actions of 'attentive' affected individuals, who completely exited their private capital accounts, are a valid benchmark for the optimal employee response, provided attentiveness is not systematically correlated with the underlying ranking of saving choices
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix Figure 4 (distribution of individual-level annual changes concentrated at the mass point of completely opting out); the paper calls the exercise 'merely a rough assessment of optimality'

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditioning the series on units with positive capital contributions in 1998 isolates those that could adjust contributions downward
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated sample construction for Figure 4

implies_edges.from: positive capital contributions in 1998 (sample inclusion)
implies_edges.to: fraction opting out of capital pension contributions

threats_discussed: the optimality benchmark is imputed from the behaviour of 'attentive' individuals rather than estimated
adjustment costs could differ systematically between attentive and inattentive individuals
robustness_checks: online Appendix Figure 4: the distribution of individual-level annual changes is concentrated at the mass point of completely opting out
unresolved_confounders: whether opting out of capital accounts really is the optimal allocation for affected workers; the paper calls the exercise 'merely a rough assessment of optimality'

estimator.value: time series of the fraction of units with positive capital contributions, among those with positive contributions in 1998 (no regression)

estimation.specification: Figure 4: extensive-margin series by workplace size category ('small' 5-19 employees, 'large' 20 or more) and, for comparison, for individual private contributions

source_table.value: Figure 4 (PDF p. 19), with the percentages stated in the text on p. 213 (PDF p. 18)
